outline.title: Does an Adaptive Off-to-On-Policy Switch Help Distillation? A Pre-Registered Negative Result on a Multimodal Transduction Task
outline.question: On the multimodal-transduction-L6-A8 seq-distill task, does switching from off-policy to on-policy training when the student's own probe invalid rate falls below a threshold lower val_invalid_rate compared with pure off-policy, pure on-policy and a fixed-step switch? If it does, does the benefit depend on the trigger responding to the student's state, and on the student's own prefixes?
outline.nugget: The pre-registered falsifying outcome was met. The adaptive-switch arm did not beat the better pure regime: pure_on_policy had the lower mean (9.04 against 12.88), so the adaptive switch was not better than the better pure regime by more than the seed–fold spread. The prediction that the adaptive arm would beat both pure regimes is therefore not supported in this configuration. The two controls meant to test why a trigger might help (yoked replay and corrupted prefixes) did not implement their intended contrasts and support no conclusion either way (see limitations). The conservative reading is that this experiment does not distinguish the switching rules.

The two controls meant to test why a trigger might help (yoked replay and corrupted prefixes) did not implement their intended contrasts and support no conclusion either way (see limitations). The adaptive-switch arm did not beat pure_on_policy on mean val_invalid_rate: pure_on_policy averaged 9.04 and the adaptive arm averaged 12.88. The pre-registered prediction that the adaptive switch would be below both pure regimes by a margin therefore fails for the on-policy endpoint. The adaptive arm had the narrower spread across seed–fold pairs.

pure_on_policy had a paired mean difference of -4.96 against off_policy_ref, but the per-pair pattern was heterogeneous. On three of five seed–fold pairs it was much better than off-policy, reaching values of 4.6, 2.6 and 4.2. On one pair it was about equal. On the remaining pair it was clearly worse (23.2 against the reference's 15.8). The direction is not uniform and the spread is large, so the sign of the mean difference is not established at this sample size.

The adaptive-switch arm had a lower mean val_invalid_rate (12.88) than off_policy_ref (14.0), a paired mean difference of -1.12. The per-seed paired differences were small and mixed in sign: four of the five seed–fold pairs were within about one point of zero, and one of those four was positive. Most of the mean improvement comes from the single pair where off_policy_ref had its highest value (18.4). The improvement is small relative to the seed–fold spread and is not robust across pairs.

The fixed-step switch arm had the highest mean val_invalid_rate of all arms (15.0), a paired mean difference of 1.0 against off_policy_ref. The paired differences were mixed in sign: three of the five seed–fold pairs were worse than the reference and two were better, and the mean difference is within the seed–fold spread. The direction of the fixed-step arm relative to pure off-policy is therefore not established. The adaptive arm (12.88) had a lower mean than the fixed-step arm, which formally satisfies the prediction that adaptive is no worse than the fixed switch. This contrast confounds trigger responsiveness with switch timing: according to self-reported diagnostics, the adaptive switches fired earlier than the fixed step on every seed, so the adaptive arm spent more of training on-policy.

According to self-reported diagnostics, the adaptive trigger fired before the forced-switch cap on all five seed–fold pairs, and no switch was forced. On-policy batches occurred only after the reported switch step. The adaptive mechanism was therefore exercised in this run, rather than every switch coming from the cap.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.purpose: Five sentences. (1) The registered question, and the finding that the pre-registered falsifying outcome was met. (2) Why it matters: when to switch from off-policy to on-policy prefixes is an open scheduling choice. (3) How: a probe-gated, one-way switch from off-policy to on-policy under a fixed forward-KL loss, compared across six arms on one synthetic task, with five seed–fold pairs per arm and a frozen scorer; lower val_invalid_rate is better. (4) Evidence: the trigger was exercised on every pair according to self-reported diagnostics, and the adaptive arm still did not beat pure on-policy. (5) The headline numbers are 12.88 for the adaptive arm against 9.04 for pure on-policy. The experiment does not distinguish the switching rules.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.purpose: Task: distil a small transformer student on a three-mode transduction task, scored by invalid-output rate. Position the work only through the approved contrasts. GKD uses a static student-data fraction. DASH-OPD and DTDD switch adaptively within rollouts. Instance-ordering curricula schedule instances rather than the policy that generates prefixes. Our move is a pre-registered falsification test of a single training-schedule switch gated by the student's probe invalid rate. State the registered prediction and the falsification criterion, then the negative headline result. Close with the contribution bullets.

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.purpose:
Group prior work by mechanism, and state for each group how this study differs.
- Off-policy SeqKD as the reference.
- On-policy and imitation-learning distillation, and the exposure-bias account.
- Static mixing (GKD) versus adaptive within-rollout triggers (DASH-OPD, DTDD).
- Instance-ordering curricula versus scheduling the prefix-generating policy.
- Separating the state distribution from the divergence: MiniLLM changes both, while this study fixes the loss at forward KL.
- Capacity and entropy caveats, which this study does not vary.
- Mask Forcing's perturbation as a method, versus this study's corruption as a control.

- Student and teacher architectures, and teacher training.
- Shared training hyperparameters and prefix sampling.

sections.heading: Results
sections.purpose:
Open with the six-arm means and seed SD; lower is better. Then go through each registered prediction in turn, stating the claim it tests before the evidence.
1. Precondition: according to self-reported diagnostics, the trigger fired before the cap on every pair, so responsiveness was exercised.
2. Adaptive at least 1.0 point below both pure regimes:
   - It fails against pure on-policy.
   - Against off-policy, the gain is small and non-robust, driven by one pair.
   - Pure on-policy versus the reference is heterogeneous across pairs, and the sign of its mean difference is not established. Apply the wording correction (limit_5).
3. Adaptive below the 8.8 hard-label baseline: no arm's mean reached it, and the baseline was not re-measured.
4. Adaptive no worse than the fixed switch: formally satisfied, but confounded with switch timing.
5. Yoked within noise of adaptive, and corrupt recovering less than half the gain: neither can be assessed, because the controls did not implement their intended contrasts. Refer to Limitations for the reasons, without restating them.
The falsifying outcome was met.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.purpose: Separate what was measured from interpretation. Measured: the registered falsifying outcome was met, and this experiment does not distinguish the switching rules. The adaptive-versus-fixed contrast confounds trigger responsiveness with switch timing. Interpretation, hedged: mode commitment is an untested competing explanation for the pure on-policy mean. The exposure-bias account remains untested here.

Conclusion

The pre-registered falsifying outcome was met. One pre-registered falsification protocol was run with six arms, each at full fidelity over five seed–fold pairs. Seed i was trained on the training prompts of cross-validation fold i and evaluated on that fold's val prompts, so seed and fold are confounded and no arm was evaluated on a single fold. The trusted metric is val_invalid_rate from the frozen scorer. The analysis reports descriptive paired mean differences against off_policy_ref, with no inferential test. Probe trajectories, switch steps and on-policy batch counts are self-reported by train.py and are not verified by the scorer. The author decided to run no further experiments. This revision therefore narrows the argument: two control comparisons and one mechanism hypothesis are withdrawn as claims and moved to the limitations.

Task multimodal-transduction-L6-A8: each input is L=6 symbols from an alphabet of 8. Three outputs are valid: the copy, the reversal, and the reversal incremented mod 8. A mixture of modes counts as invalid.

Task multimodal-transduction-L6-A8: each input is L=6 symbols from an alphabet of 8. Three outputs are valid: the copy, the reversal, and the reversal incremented mod 8. A mixture of modes counts as invalid.

Every possible input is shuffled once. Five folds of 500 prompts each are cut from the start of that order, the next 2000 prompts form the held-out test set, and the teacher trains on the rest. A run on one fold validates on that fold and trains on the prompts of the other four.
The metric val_invalid_rate is the percentage of greedy student decodes on a validation fold that match none of the valid outputs. Lower is better. Each validation fold holds 500 prompts.

The student is a frozen-architecture pre-norm causal transformer with d_model 32, 2 layers and 2 heads. The frozen teacher has d_model 96 and 2 layers, trained for 8000 steps on inputs disjoint from the fold pool and the test set.

The teacher is trained once with a fixed seed for 8000 steps of AdamW at lr 1e-3 and batch 128. Each training target is one valid output chosen uniformly at random from the three modes, and the loss is cross-entropy over output positions.
Every arm trains for 3000 steps with batch 64 using AdamW at lr 0.003. The loss is forward KL between teacher and student next-token distributions at temperature 1.0 over output positions.

Training prefixes are sampled, not decoded greedily: each batch draws its output sequences from either the teacher or the student at sampling temperature 1.0, and on_policy_frac is the probability that a batch uses the student.
The probe batch is a fixed subset of 256 training prompts, drawn once per run from a generator seeded with 10000 plus the run seed. The probe and the evaluation decode greedily.
The off_policy_ref arm runs the unmodified script with on_policy_frac 0, so the teacher samples every training prefix.
The pure_on_policy arm sets on_policy_frac to 1 throughout, so the student samples every prefix and the teacher labels it.
The fixed_switch_1500 arm uses on_policy_frac 0 before step 1500 and 1.0 afterwards. A probe runs every 100 steps for logging only.

In the adaptive_tau25 arm, a probe greedily decodes 256 training prompts every 100 steps. When the probe invalid rate falls below 25%, on_policy_frac switches from 0 to 1.0. The switch is forced at step 1500 if the trigger has not fired.

The yoked_replay arm first replays the adaptive run for the seed to find its firing step. It then trains a fresh student from training seed seed+1000 and switches to on_policy_frac 1.0 at exactly that step, ignoring the probe.

The corrupt_prefix arm uses the adaptive trigger and cap. After the switch, it samples student rollouts to measure per-token error p, then trains on ground-truth outputs (mode chosen uniformly) with each symbol substituted at rate p.

Per-token error p is the smallest number of positions at which a sampled student rollout differs from any valid output, divided by the output length. It is computed on each post-switch batch. Corruption draws use a generator seeded with 20000 plus the run seed.
Each arm ran five seeds (zero through four) over five cross-validation folds at full fidelity. Run records list fold indices alongside seed indices, so seed and fold vary together.
Each arm's run record lists 5 training attempts for its five seeds.
Each full-fidelity run had a time budget of 1200 seconds.

Its post-switch prefixes were also exact ground truth rather than teacher samples. Its mean paired gain is also dominated by the same outlying reference pair as the adaptive gain. It is no longer treated as a test of whether the benefit needs the student's own prefixes; that question is unanswered.

Withdrawn claim (claim_yoked_matches_or_beats): the yoked replay arm trained on different seeds from the reference and adaptive arms. Its recorded per-seed differences are therefore not paired observations, and only a difference of means can be reported. That difference does not separate yoked from adaptive given the yoked arm's large spread, and the yoked students switched in different training states from their adaptive sources. Whether online responsiveness adds value beyond switch timing is untested.

Withdrawn claim (claim_variance_mechanism_hypothesis): the previous version proposed that more training on student-generated or noisy prefixes yields more seed-dependent outcomes. The data contradict this premise. The adaptive and yoked arms had identical on-policy batch counts yet very different spreads, and with five values per arm the spread estimates cannot rank variance. No mode-commitment diagnostic was recorded, and no mechanism for the dispersion is claimed.

The pre-registered falsifying outcome was met. The adaptive-switch arm did not beat the better pure regime: pure_on_policy had the lower mean (9.04 against 12.88), so the adaptive switch was not better than the better pure regime by more than the seed–fold spread. The prediction that the adaptive arm would beat both pure regimes is therefore not supported in this configuration. The two controls meant to test why a trigger might help (yoked replay and corrupted prefixes) did not implement their intended contrasts and support no conclusion either way (see limitations). The conservative reading is that this experiment does not distinguish the switching rules.

The adaptive-switch arm did not beat pure_on_policy on mean val_invalid_rate: pure_on_policy averaged 9.04 and the adaptive arm averaged 12.88. The pre-registered prediction that the adaptive switch would be below both pure regimes by a margin therefore fails for the on-policy endpoint. The adaptive arm had the narrower spread across seed–fold pairs.
Single synthetic task, single tiny fixed student, single divergence. The results do not generalise beyond this setting.

Run verdicts are recorded as 'discarded' and the protocol outcome is 'unreviewed'. The author has decided not to run further experiments, so the requested reruns (cross-yoked seeds, replayed-rate corruption, mode-share diagnostics, more seeds) were not done.

A reader may take it as a selling point for the adaptive arm. limit_4 states that 'with five values per arm the spread estimates cannot rank variance', so headline placement over-weights a descriptive SD comparison the paper itself disclaims.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.body: On the multimodal-transduction-L6-A8 seq-distill task, we asked whether switching from off-policy to on-policy training, once the student's own probe invalid rate falls below a threshold, lowers val_invalid_rate compared with pure off-policy, pure on-policy and a fixed-step switch [scope_question]. The pre-registered falsifying outcome was met: the adaptive-switch arm did not beat the better pure regime, so the experiment does not distinguish the switching rules [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. We ran one pre-registered protocol with six arms, each over five seed–fold pairs, with the same learning rate, temperature, forward-KL loss and step budget in every arm and val_invalid_rate (lower is better) computed by a frozen scorer [scope_method]. According to self-reported diagnostics, the adaptive trigger fired before the forced-switch cap on all five seed–fold pairs, so the adaptive mechanism was exercised in this run [claim_trigger_exercised]. The adaptive arm still did not beat pure_on_policy on mean val_invalid_rate, which averaged 12.88 for the adaptive arm against 9.04 for pure_on_policy [claim_adaptive_not_below_pure_on].

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.body:
The task, multimodal-transduction-L6-A8, gives the student an input of L=6 symbols from an alphabet of 8, and three outputs are valid: the copy, the reversal, and the reversal incremented mod 8 [setup_task]. An output that mixes modes counts as invalid [setup_task].

GKD trains students on a mixture of fixed and self-generated sequences with a static student-data fraction [related_gkd]. We keep that fraction knob and switch it once during training, conditioned on the student's probe invalid rate [related_gkd]. DASH-OPD and DTDD switch adaptively between teacher and student within rollouts using discrepancy signals, and their abstracts do not describe yoked or corrupted-prefix controls [related_adaptive_triggers]. Our study instead makes a single, one-way, training-schedule switch gated by a probe invalid rate [related_adaptive_triggers]. Instance-level curriculum distillation orders training instances using an earlier student snapshot, whereas we schedule the policy that generates prefixes rather than the order of instances [related_curriculum].

We ask whether, on the multimodal-transduction-L6-A8 seq-distill task, switching from off-policy to on-policy training when the student's own probe invalid rate falls below a threshold lowers val_invalid_rate compared with pure off-policy, pure on-policy and a fixed-step switch [scope_question]. If it does, we ask whether the benefit depends on the trigger responding to the student's state, and on the student's own prefixes [scope_question].

The registered prediction was that adaptive_tau25 is at least 1.0 point below both pure regimes and below the 8.8 hard-label baseline, and no worse than fixed_switch_1500 [setup_prediction]. The prediction further held that yoked_replay is within noise of adaptive or worse, and that corrupt_prefix recovers less than half of the adaptive gain over off_policy_ref [setup_prediction]. The registered falsification states that the hypothesis fails if adaptive_tau25 does not beat the better of off_policy_ref and pure_on_policy by more than the seed standard deviation, or if both yoked_replay and corrupt_prefix match it [setup_falsification]. A trigger that fires only through the cap on every seed would leave responsiveness untested [setup_falsification].

The pre-registered falsifying outcome was met: pure_on_policy had the lower mean (9.04 against 12.88), so the adaptive switch did not beat the better pure regime by more than the seed–fold spread [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. The yoked-replay and corrupted-prefix controls did not implement their intended contrasts, so the conservative reading is that this experiment does not distinguish the switching rules [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. The prediction that the adaptive switch would sit below both pure regimes by a margin therefore fails for the on-policy endpoint of val_invalid_rate [claim_adaptive_not_below_pure_on]. The adaptive arm did have the narrower spread across seed–fold pairs [claim_adaptive_not_below_pure_on].

sections.heading: Related Work
sections.body:
Sequence-level knowledge distillation [arXiv:1606.07947] trains the student on teacher-generated outputs and is the canonical off-policy baseline [related_seqkd]. Our reference arm follows this off-policy setting and applies word-level distillation on teacher-sampled prefixes [related_seqkd].

Imitation-learning distillation [arXiv:2009.07253] [doi:10.1007/s00521-025-11162-0] treats the teacher as an oracle on student-visited states, which addresses exposure bias [related_imitation]. We designed a corrupted-prefix control to test this exposure-bias account [related_imitation]. The control's corruption rate tracked its own student's rollout error instead of the adaptive student's, so the control yields no conclusion and the account remains untested here [related_imitation].

GKD [arXiv:2306.13649] trains students on a mixture of fixed and self-generated sequences, with a static student-data fraction [related_gkd]. We keep that fraction knob and switch it once during training, conditioned on the student's probe invalid rate [related_gkd]. DASH-OPD [arXiv:2607.29078] and DTDD [arXiv:2610.19302] instead switch adaptively between teacher and student within rollouts, using discrepancy signals [related_adaptive_triggers]. Our switch is a single, one-way change in the training schedule, gated by a probe invalid rate [related_adaptive_triggers]. The abstracts of these two methods do not describe yoked or corrupted-prefix controls [related_adaptive_triggers].

Instance-level curriculum distillation [arXiv:2106.10885v1] orders training instances using an earlier student snapshot [related_curriculum]. Our study schedules the policy that generates prefixes and leaves the order of instances unchanged [related_curriculum].

MiniLLM [arXiv:2306.08543] changes two factors at once: the divergence, which becomes reverse KL, and the sampling distribution [related_minillm]. We hold the forward-KL loss fixed and vary only the prefix source and its schedule [related_minillm]. A controlled study on GSM8K [arXiv:2605.22731v1] argues that the state distribution under supervision matters alongside the loss [related_state_distribution]. Our study varies only the state source, and does so on a non-language transduction task [related_state_distribution].

Prior work [arXiv:2409.12512] reports that student-generated outputs are costly and hard to optimise when the student is much smaller than the teacher [related_capacity]. We use one fixed small student and do not vary the capacity gap [related_capacity]. Entropy-aware on-policy distillation [arXiv:2603.07079] reports that reverse-KL signals become unstable under high teacher entropy [related_entropy]. Our teacher models a three-mode distribution, but we did not measure or vary teacher entropy [related_entropy].

Mask Forcing [arXiv:2609.09123] perturbs student self-rollouts in video diffusion distillation [related_mask_forcing]. Our corrupted-prefix arm perturbs ground-truth discrete prefixes and serves only as a control, with no claim as a method [related_mask_forcing].

sections.heading: Setup and Pre-Registered Protocol
sections.body:
We ran one pre-registered falsification protocol with six arms, each at full fidelity over five seed–fold pairs [scope_method]. Seed i was trained on the training prompts of cross-validation fold i and evaluated on that fold's val prompts, so seed and fold are confounded and no arm was evaluated on a single fold [scope_method]. Learning rate, temperature, forward-KL loss and step budget were the same in every arm, and the student architecture and teacher were frozen [scope_method]. The arms were off_policy_ref (the reference), pure_on_policy, a fixed switch to fully on-policy at a mid-run step, and an adaptive arm that switches to fully on-policy once the greedy invalid rate on a training-prompt probe batch drops below threshold, with a forced-switch cap [scope_method]. Two further arms completed the set: a yoked replay that switches at the adaptive arm's firing step but trains on a different seed, and a corrupted-prefix arm that uses the same trigger but replaces post-switch prefixes with ground truth under token substitution [scope_method]. The trusted metric is val_invalid_rate from the frozen scorer, and the analysis reports descriptive paired mean differences against off_policy_ref, with no inferential test [scope_method]. Probe trajectories, switch steps and on-policy batch counts are self-reported by train.py and are not verified by the scorer [scope_method]. The author decided to run no further experiments, so this revision narrows the argument: two control comparisons and one mechanism hypothesis are withdrawn as claims and moved to the limitations [scope_method].

In the task multimodal-transduction-L6-A8, each input is L=6 symbols from an alphabet of 8 [setup_task]. Three outputs are valid: the copy, the reversal, and the reversal incremented mod 8 [setup_task]. A mixture of modes counts as invalid [setup_task]. Every possible input is shuffled once, and five folds of 500 prompts each are cut from the start of that order [setup_folds]. The next 2000 prompts form the held-out test set, and the teacher trains on the rest [setup_folds]. A run on one fold validates on that fold and trains on the prompts of the other four [setup_folds]. The metric val_invalid_rate is the percentage of greedy student decodes on a validation fold that match none of the valid outputs, and lower is better [setup_metric]. Each validation fold holds 500 prompts [setup_metric].

The student is a frozen-architecture pre-norm causal transformer with d_model 32, 2 layers and 2 heads [setup_models]. The frozen teacher has d_model 96 and 2 layers, trained for 8000 steps on inputs disjoint from the fold pool and the test set [setup_models]. The teacher is trained once with a fixed seed for 8000 steps of AdamW at lr 1e-3 and batch 128 [setup_teacher_training]. Each teacher training target is one valid output chosen uniformly at random from the three modes, and the loss is cross-entropy over output positions [setup_teacher_training].

Every arm trains for 3000 steps with batch 64 using AdamW at lr 0.003 [setup_training]. The loss is forward KL between teacher and student next-token distributions at temperature 1.0 over output positions [setup_training]. Training prefixes are sampled rather than decoded greedily: each batch draws its output sequences from either the teacher or the student at sampling temperature 1.0 [setup_prefix_sampling]. The quantity on_policy_frac is the probability that a batch uses the student [setup_prefix_sampling].

The probe batch is a fixed subset of 256 training prompts, drawn once per run from a generator seeded with 10000 plus the run seed [setup_probe]. The probe and the evaluation decode greedily [setup_probe]. The off_policy_ref arm runs the unmodified script with on_policy_frac 0, so the teacher samples every training prefix [setup_arm_offpolicy]. The pure_on_policy arm sets on_policy_frac to 1 throughout, so the student samples every prefix and the teacher labels it [setup_arm_pureon]. The fixed_switch_1500 arm uses on_policy_frac 0 before step 1500 and 1.0 afterwards, with a probe every 100 steps for logging only [setup_arm_fixed].

In the adaptive_tau25 arm, a probe greedily decodes 256 training prompts every 100 steps [setup_arm_adaptive]. When the probe invalid rate falls below 25%, on_policy_frac switches from 0 to 1.0 [setup_arm_adaptive]. The switch is forced at step 1500 if the trigger has not fired [setup_arm_adaptive]. The yoked_replay arm first replays the adaptive run for the seed to find its firing step [setup_arm_yoked]. It then trains a fresh student from training seed seed+1000 and switches to on_policy_frac 1.0 at exactly that step, ignoring the probe [setup_arm_yoked].

The corrupt_prefix arm uses the adaptive trigger and cap [setup_arm_corrupt]. After the switch, it samples student rollouts to measure per-token error p, then trains on ground-truth outputs (mode chosen uniformly) with each symbol substituted at rate p [setup_arm_corrupt]. Per-token error p is the smallest number of positions at which a sampled student rollout differs from any valid output, divided by the output length [setup_token_error]. It is computed on each post-switch batch, and corruption draws use a generator seeded with 20000 plus the run seed [setup_token_error].

Each arm ran five seeds (zero through four) over five cross-validation folds at full fidelity [setup_seeds_folds]. Run records list fold indices alongside seed indices, so seed and fold vary together [setup_seeds_folds]. Each arm's run record lists 5 training attempts for its five seeds [setup_attempts]. Each full-fidelity run had a time budget of 1200 seconds [setup_budget]. The frozen protocol records the software environment: Python 3.12.9, torch 2.11.0 and numpy 2.2.6 [setup_environment].

The analysis computes, for each arm, per-seed paired mean differences against off_policy_ref, read descriptively beside the seed spread, with no inferential test [setup_analysis]. The profile declares a val_invalid_rate of 8.8 for a hard-label training baseline [setup_baseline]. That baseline was not re-run in this protocol [setup_baseline].

The registered prediction was that adaptive_tau25 is at least 1.0 point below both pure regimes and below the 8.8 hard-label baseline, and no worse than fixed_switch_1500 [setup_prediction]. It further predicted that yoked_replay is within noise of adaptive or worse, and that corrupt_prefix recovers less than half of the adaptive gain over off_policy_ref [setup_prediction]. Under the registered falsification, the hypothesis fails if adaptive_tau25 does not beat the better of off_policy_ref and pure_on_policy by more than the seed standard deviation, or if both yoked_replay and corrupt_prefix match it [setup_falsification]. A trigger that fires only through the cap on every seed leaves responsiveness untested [setup_falsification].

Attempts made outside the registered protocol, if any, are not reported [limit_15]. Hardware is not recorded, so the time budget is not tied to a machine [limit_15]. Setup details absent from the setup statements are not part of the recorded evidence [limit_15]. Implementation details not restated in the setup statements are fixed in the frozen scorer and the versioned training scripts, and are not described further here [limit_16].

sections.heading: Results
sections.body:
Mean validation invalid rate (%, lower is better) over five seeds, with seed SD in parentheses, was 14.0 (3.234192) for off_policy_ref, 9.04 (8.478679) for pure_on_policy, 15.0 (3.896152) for fixed_switch_1500, 12.88 (2.229798) for adaptive_tau25, 11.0 (8.866792) for yoked_replay and 12.76 (6.582401) for corrupt_prefix [claim_all_arms_observation].

The precondition for testing trigger responsiveness held: according to self-reported diagnostics, the adaptive trigger fired before the forced-switch cap on all five seed–fold pairs, and no switch was forced [claim_trigger_exercised]. On-policy batches occurred only after the reported switch step [claim_trigger_exercised]. The adaptive mechanism was therefore exercised in this run, rather than every switch coming from the cap [claim_trigger_exercised].

The pre-registered prediction that the adaptive switch would sit below both pure regimes by a margin fails for the on-policy endpoint, because pure_on_policy averaged 9.04 and the adaptive arm averaged 12.88 [claim_adaptive_not_below_pure_on]. The adaptive arm had the narrower spread across seed–fold pairs [claim_adaptive_not_below_pure_on].

Against off_policy_ref, the same prediction meets only a small gain: the adaptive arm had a lower mean val_invalid_rate (12.88 against 14.0), a paired mean difference of -1.12 [claim_adaptive_vs_offpolicy]. The per-seed paired differences were small and mixed in sign, with four of the five seed–fold pairs within about one point of zero and one of those four positive [claim_adaptive_vs_offpolicy]. Most of the mean improvement comes from the single pair where off_policy_ref had its highest value (18.4) [claim_adaptive_vs_offpolicy]. The improvement is therefore small relative to the seed–fold spread and is not robust across pairs [claim_adaptive_vs_offpolicy].

The pure on-policy endpoint had a paired mean difference of -4.96 against off_policy_ref, but the per-pair pattern was heterogeneous [claim_pure_on_high_variance]. On three of five seed–fold pairs it was much better than off-policy, reaching values of 4.6, 2.6 and 4.2 [claim_pure_on_high_variance]. On one pair it was about equal, and on the remaining pair it was clearly worse (23.2 against the reference's 15.8) [claim_pure_on_high_variance]. This per-pair count corrects an earlier wording that placed the mean advantage on a 'minority' of seeds, since three of five pairs were much better, one about equal and one worse [limit_5]. Because the direction is not uniform and the spread is large, the sign of the mean difference is not established at this sample size [claim_pure_on_high_variance].

The prediction that the adaptive arm would fall below the profile's declared hard-label baseline is not met, since no arm's mean reached that baseline [limit_12]. That baseline was not re-measured in this study, so the comparison is indicative only [limit_12].

For the prediction that the adaptive arm would be no worse than the fixed switch, the reference point is weak: the fixed-step switch arm had the highest mean val_invalid_rate of all arms (15.0), a paired mean difference of 1.0 against off_policy_ref [claim_fixed_switch_worse]. Its paired differences were mixed in sign, with three of the five seed–fold pairs worse than the reference and two better, and the mean difference lies within the seed–fold spread [claim_fixed_switch_worse]. The direction of the fixed-step arm relative to pure off-policy is therefore not established [claim_fixed_switch_worse]. The adaptive arm (12.88) had a lower mean than the fixed-step arm, which formally satisfies the prediction that adaptive is no worse than the fixed switch [claim_fixed_switch_worse]. This contrast confounds trigger responsiveness with switch timing, because self-reported diagnostics show the adaptive switches fired earlier than the fixed step on every seed, so the adaptive arm spent more of training on-policy [claim_fixed_switch_worse].

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.body:
The pre-registered falsifying outcome was met [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. The adaptive-switch arm did not beat the better pure regime: pure_on_policy had the lower mean (9.04 against 12.88), so the adaptive switch was not better than the better pure regime by more than the seed–fold spread [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. The prediction that the adaptive arm would beat both pure regimes is therefore not supported in this configuration [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. sections.heading: Limitations
sections.body:
Seed i was trained and evaluated on cross-validation fold i, so training prompts, probe prompts and the val set all change with the seed [limit_1]. The spread across seeds is therefore seed-plus-fold variation, and nothing was evaluated on a single fold [limit_1]. Paired differences are paired against the reference on both seed and fold [limit_1].

Each arm has only five seed–fold pairs, and we ran no inferential test and computed no interval on any paired difference [limit_6]. Each value comes from a single evaluation on a few hundred val prompts, and the binomial evaluation noise is of the same order as the adaptive-versus-reference mean difference [limit_6]. 'Within noise' was never quantified [limit_6].

We ran only one adaptive setting (one probe threshold, full on-policy target) and one fixed switch step [limit_7]. The threshold sweep, partial targets, the static mixed-fraction arm and the other fixed steps were omitted [limit_7]. The yoked and corrupt arms also do not match the other arms in compute: the yoked arm spends replay compute and the corrupt arm discards student rollouts [limit_9]. No compute-matched total was recorded [limit_9].

Probe trajectories, switch steps, on-policy batch counts and per-token error rates are self-reported by train.py and are not verified by the scorer [limit_10]. The probe uses training prompts, not val [limit_10]. The study covers a single synthetic task, a single tiny fixed student and a single divergence, and the results do not generalise beyond this setting [limit_11].

Run verdicts are recorded as 'discarded' and the protocol outcome as 'unreviewed' [limit_13]. The author has decided not to run further experiments, so the requested reruns (cross-yoked seeds, replayed-rate corruption, mode-share diagnostics, more seeds) were not done [limit_13].

We withdraw the claim that the corrupted-prefix control recovers the adaptive gain (claim_corrupt_recovers_gain), because that control set its substitution rate from its own student's sampled rollout error instead of the adaptive student's [limit_2]. That student drifted to higher rollout error than the adaptive student on every seed (self-reported student_rollout_tokerr_mean), so the control did not implement the specified matched noise level [limit_2]. Its post-switch prefixes were also exact ground truth rather than teacher samples, and its mean paired gain is dominated by the same outlying reference pair as the adaptive gain [limit_2]. The control is no longer treated as a test of whether the benefit needs the student's own prefixes, and that question is unanswered [limit_2].

We withdraw the claim that the yoked replay arm matches or beats the adaptive arm (claim_yoked_matches_or_beats), because the yoked arm trained on different seeds from the reference and adaptive arms [limit_3]. Its recorded per-seed differences are therefore not paired observations, and only a difference of means can be reported [limit_3]. That difference does not separate yoked from adaptive given the yoked arm's large spread, and the yoked students switched in different training states from their adaptive sources [limit_3]. Whether online responsiveness adds value beyond switch timing is untested [limit_3].

We also withdraw the variance-mechanism hypothesis (claim_variance_mechanism_hypothesis), which in the previous version proposed that more training on student-generated or noisy prefixes yields more seed-dependent outcomes [limit_4]. The data contradict this premise: the adaptive and yoked arms had identical on-policy batch counts yet very different spreads [limit_4]. With five values per arm, the spread estimates cannot rank variance [limit_4]. No mode-commitment diagnostic was recorded, and we claim no mechanism for the dispersion [limit_4].

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.body:
We asked whether a probe-gated switch from off-policy to on-policy training lowers val_invalid_rate on this task, and the pre-registered falsifying outcome was met: the adaptive-switch arm did not beat the better pure regime, so this experiment does not distinguish the switching rules [claim_hypothesis_not_supported]. Pure_on_policy averaged 9.04 and the adaptive arm averaged 12.88 (lower is better), although the adaptive arm had the narrower spread across seed–fold pairs [claim_adaptive_not_below_pure_on].

The scope is one synthetic task with one tiny fixed student and one divergence, so the results do not generalise beyond this setting [limit_11]. The author has decided not to run further experiments, so the requested reruns (cross-yoked seeds, replayed-rate corruption, mode-share diagnostics, more seeds) were not done and remain the next steps [limit_13].

review.title: Does an Adaptive Off-to-On-Policy Switch Help Distillation? A Pre-Registered Negative Result on a Multimodal Transduction Task

reviews.summary: The paper reports a pre-registered six-arm experiment on a synthetic transduction task: L=6 symbols over an 8-symbol alphabet, with three valid output modes. A 2-layer d_model-32 student is distilled with forward KL from a frozen teacher. The question is whether a probe-gated, one-way switch from off-policy to on-policy prefixes (adaptive_tau25) lowers val_invalid_rate against three comparators: pure off-policy, pure on-policy and a fixed switch at step 1500. Two mechanism controls were planned, a yoked replay and a corrupted-prefix arm. With 5 seed–fold pairs per arm, the adaptive arm (12.88, SD 2.23) did not beat pure_on_policy (9.04, SD 8.48). Its -1.12 paired gain over off_policy_ref (14.0) is driven by one pair. The registered falsification is therefore met. Both controls were mis-implemented and their claims were withdrawn. Pure on-policy is strongly heterogeneous across pairs, and the sign of its advantage is not established. The authors conclude, conservatively, that the experiment does not distinguish switching rules. The write-up is unusually honest about its failures. However, the experiment yields almost no insight: the controls that would have produced the mechanistic content are void, the comparator effects are within binomial noise, and the scope is a single tiny synthetic setting.
strengths: The protocol was pre-registered with an explicit numeric prediction (adaptive ≥1.0 point below both pure regimes and below 8.8). The falsification rule ('does not beat the better of off_policy_ref and pure_on_policy by more than the seed SD') is applied as written, not reinterpreted after the fact.

Means and SDs are reported for all six arms (Results, first paragraph). Paired differences are described at the per-pair level, for example that the adaptive gain comes mostly from the single pair where off_policy_ref was 18.4. This exposes the fragility of the mean instead of hiding it.
The precondition for testing responsiveness is checked rather than assumed: the trigger fired before the cap on all 5 pairs. The authors also flag that this evidence is self-reported by train.py.

The Limitations section explicitly withdraws three earlier claims (claim_corrupt_recovers_gain, claim_yoked_matches_or_beats, claim_variance_mechanism_hypothesis) and states concrete reasons for each. The reasons are a mismatched corruption rate, non-paired seeds, and identical on-policy batch counts with different spreads.

Several design details are stated precisely enough to re-implement the arms: the probe seed (10000+seed), the corruption seed (20000+seed), the definition of per-token error p, and the fold construction (5×500 prompts plus a 2000-prompt test set).
weaknesses: Self-consistency, Abstract and Conclusion. The sentence 'although the adaptive arm had the narrower spread across seed–fold pairs' (repeated in the Introduction and Results) is presented as a mitigating positive. It contradicts the Limitations, which state 'with five values per arm the spread estimates cannot rank variance'. Either drop the spread claim from the abstract and conclusion, or support it, for example with a bootstrap interval on the SD ratio or with more seeds.

Quality, Results. 'The adaptive switch did not beat the better pure regime' rests on pure_on_policy being the better pure regime. The paper itself says 'the sign of the mean difference [pure_on vs off_policy] is not established at this sample size.' The falsification holds against either reference, since -1.12 is smaller than both SDs. The text should say this explicitly instead of framing the result as 'pure_on_policy had the lower mean (9.04 against 12.88)'. Report the per-pair table (5 values × 6 arms) so readers can verify both comparisons.

Quality, Results and Limitations. No per-pair values are tabulated, yet the text cites individual values (18.4, 23.2, 15.8, 4.6, 2.6, 4.2). Sentence-level traceability requires a table of all 30 val_invalid_rate values with seed and fold indices.

Quality, Setup. The teacher's own val_invalid_rate is never reported. Without it, the reader cannot tell whether 9–15% invalid is near the teacher ceiling or far from it. The relevance of the 8.8 hard-label baseline is also unclear, and that baseline was not re-run ('That baseline was not re-measured'). Fix: report teacher invalid rate and per-mode output shares on each fold, and re-run the hard-label baseline under the same seed–fold protocol.

Quality, Limitations ('binomial evaluation noise is of the same order as the adaptive-versus-reference mean difference'). At p≈0.13 with n=500, the binomial SE is about 1.5 points, which matches the 1.12 gain. 'Within noise' was never quantified, yet the registered falsification depends on it. Significance and originality, whole paper. The two controls that carried the mechanistic question, 'does the benefit depend on the trigger responding... and on the student's own prefixes', both failed by design. The yoked arm used seed+1000, so it was not paired. The corrupt arm used its own student's error rate and ground-truth rather than teacher prefixes. Quality, Results (fixed-switch paragraph). The confound is real but trivially entailed. Discussion. The one potentially insightful observation is left as untested speculation: pure_on_policy is bimodal, with three pairs at 2.6–4.6 and one at 23.2, and the authors suggest mode commitment. Both mechanistic controls are withdrawn as mis-implemented, and no inferential statistics are reported. The paper is candid and internally mostly consistent. Its substantive content is one null result in one tiny setting, and its key secondary comparisons are uninformative by the authors' own account.
strengths: Pre-registered prediction and falsification criteria are stated verbatim in Setup, and the Results walk through each clause (both pure regimes, the 8.8 hard-label baseline, the fixed switch) instead of cherry-picking.

The precondition check that the adaptive trigger fired before the step-1500 cap on all five pairs is reported. It rules out the degenerate case where 'adaptive' collapses to a fixed switch, though it is self-reported.

Per-pair decomposition of the paired differences gives concrete numbers: pure_on_policy is 4.6, 2.6 and 4.2 on three pairs and 23.2 vs 15.8 on one, and the adaptive gain is dominated by the single 18.4 reference pair. This honestly undercuts the mean-based reading.

Limitations are explicit and specific. Seed–fold confounding, the binomial noise scale, the withdrawn controls with concrete implementation reasons (the corruption rate tracked the wrong student; yoked runs on unpaired seeds), and self-reported diagnostics are all named.
Abstract and conclusions stay within scope: single task, single student, single divergence, no generalization claim.
weaknesses: Significance (whole paper): the contribution reduces to 'on one 6-token synthetic task with a 2-layer d=32 student, one adaptive threshold did not beat pure on-policy over 5 noisy pairs'. A practitioner learns nothing actionable. The pure_on_policy SD of 8.48 means the non-result is also not a confident negative. Quality, Results ('so the adaptive switch did not beat the better pure regime by more than the seed–fold spread'): the falsification is met trivially because adaptive is worse on the mean, but the paper never states which SD it uses as the margin. With n=5 and binomial noise per evaluation of about ±1.5 points at 500 prompts, no difference here is resolved. Fix: report bootstrap or paired-t intervals on every paired difference and per-pair raw values in a table.

Quality, Setup ('seed and fold are confounded'): this design choice is not motivated and inflates spread. Self-consistency, Abstract vs Discussion ('the experiment does not distinguish the switching rules'): this conservative conclusion conflicts with the Results' reading that adaptive 'formally satisfies' no worse than fixed and shows a -1.12 gain vs off-policy. Quality, Limitations (withdrawn yoked and corrupt claims): two of six arms (a third of compute) are acknowledged as not implementing their contrasts. Quality, Results/Limitations (the 8.8 hard-label baseline): this baseline is comparable to or better than every distillation arm except pure on-policy, yet it was not re-run. Self-consistency (Abstract, last sentence; Discussion, first paragraph): 'did not beat the better pure regime by more than the seed–fold spread' is never computed against the registered criterion. The criterion is to beat the better arm by more than the seed SD, and which SD is meant is unspecified. Fix: state the threshold value used and the arithmetic.

Abstract: it opens with the result framing but omits that both mechanism controls failed to implement their contrasts. Readers reach the Limitations before learning that two of six arms are uninterpretable. Fix: state in the abstract that the yoked and corrupt controls were invalid.

Design flaw (Setup, sentence 'trains a fresh student from training seed seed+1000'): the yoked arm was unpaired by construction. This is a pre-registration design error, not an execution slip, and it undermines the central question of whether responsiveness matters. Fix: run cross-yoked seeds on the same seed and fold.

Limitations, binomial-noise sentence ('of the same order as the adaptive-versus-reference mean difference'): the claim is asserted, not shown. With 500 prompts at about 13%, the SE is about 1.5 points. Fix: report this number explicitly.

Reproducibility (Setup, 'Implementation details not restated… are fixed in the frozen scorer… and are not described further here'): this sentence and 'Setup details absent from the setup statements are not part of the recorded evidence' are boilerplate that defers to unreleased artifacts. Fix: release the code or remove these sentences.

Clarity: the Introduction largely duplicates the Related Work paragraphs (GKD, DASH-OPD/DTDD, curriculum) and the Setup's prediction and falsification text nearly verbatim. Leftover drafting notes and the 'evidence bindings' footer remain in the submission. Fix: remove the duplication and the drafting notes.

Related Work (DASH-OPD/DTDD sentence): 'Their abstracts do not describe yoked or corrupted-prefix controls' positions the paper on controls that it then reports as failed. That novelty claim no longer holds and should be cut.

Non-obvious angle not pursued: the mode-commitment explanation for pure_on's bimodal outcomes is the most interesting possibility in the data. A cheap post-hoc mode-share count on the existing checkpoints would test it, but none was done.
strengths: The protocol was pre-registered with an explicit numeric prediction (adaptive ≥1.0 point below both pure regimes and below 8.8). The falsification rule ('does not beat the better of off_policy_ref and pure_on_policy by more than the seed SD') is applied as written, not reinterpreted after the fact.

Means and SDs are reported for all six arms (Results, first paragraph). Paired differences are described at the per-pair level, for example that the adaptive gain comes mostly from the single pair where off_policy_ref was 18.4. This exposes the fragility of the mean instead of hiding it.
The precondition for testing responsiveness is checked rather than assumed: the trigger fired before the cap on all 5 pairs. The authors also flag that this evidence is self-reported by train.py.

The Limitations section explicitly withdraws three earlier claims (claim_corrupt_recovers_gain, claim_yoked_matches_or_beats, claim_variance_mechanism_hypothesis) and states concrete reasons for each. The reasons are a mismatched corruption rate, non-paired seeds, and identical on-policy batch counts with different spreads.

Several design details are stated precisely enough to re-implement the arms: the probe seed (10000+seed), the corruption seed (20000+seed), the definition of per-token error p, and the fold construction (5×500 prompts plus a 2000-prompt test set).

Pre-registered prediction and falsification criteria are stated verbatim in Setup, and the Results walk through each clause (both pure regimes, the 8.8 hard-label baseline, the fixed switch) instead of cherry-picking.

The precondition check that the adaptive trigger fired before the step-1500 cap on all five pairs is reported. It rules out the degenerate case where 'adaptive' collapses to a fixed switch, though it is self-reported.

Per-pair decomposition of the paired differences gives concrete numbers: pure_on_policy is 4.6, 2.6 and 4.2 on three pairs and 23.2 vs 15.8 on one, and the adaptive gain is dominated by the single 18.4 reference pair. This honestly undercuts the mean-based reading.

Limitations are explicit and specific. Seed–fold confounding, the binomial noise scale, the withdrawn controls with concrete implementation reasons (the corruption rate tracked the wrong student; yoked runs on unpaired seeds), and self-reported diagnostics are all named.
Abstract and conclusions stay within scope: single task, single student, single divergence, no generalization claim.
Pre-registered prediction and falsification criteria are stated verbatim (Setup), and the paper reports honestly that the falsifying outcome was met rather than reframing it.

Per-pair breakdowns go beyond means. For pure_on_policy: 4.6, 2.6 and 4.2 on three pairs, about equal on one, 23.2 vs 15.8 on one. For adaptive vs reference: four of five pairs within about one point, with the gain driven by the 18.4 reference outlier. These breakdowns prevent overreading the mean differences.

The paper withdraws three earlier claims (corrupt-prefix recovery, yoked match, variance mechanism) and gives concrete reasons for each. For corrupt_prefix, the corruption rate was set from the arm's own student rather than the adaptive student. For yoked_replay, the training seeds differ, so pairing is broken.

The precondition check is stated: the trigger fired before the cap on all five pairs, so responsiveness was at least exercised. The confound between adaptive timing and on-policy duration in the fixed-switch contrast is acknowledged.
Reproduction detail is high: architectures, optimiser, learning rates, probe seeding, fold construction, corruption seeding and software versions are all given.
questions: What is the teacher's val_invalid_rate on each fold? What output-mode distribution does the teacher produce under greedy decoding?
For the yoked arm, did seed i+1000 train and evaluate on fold i? If so, it is paired on fold, though not on seed. Why can the per-fold differences not be reported?
At which step did the adaptive trigger fire on each of the 5 pairs? How does the fraction of steps spent on-policy compare across adaptive, fixed and yoked?
Can you report greedy-decode mode shares for the pure_on_policy pairs? This would test whether the 23.2 pair is a mode-mixing failure and the 2.6–4.6 pairs are single-mode commitment.
Why was the 2000-prompt held-out test set not used for evaluation? It would reduce binomial noise roughly by a factor of two.
Given that both pre-registered controls are void, what in this paper would change a practitioner's choice between off-policy, on-policy and switched schedules?
What is the teacher's own val_invalid_rate and output-mode distribution? Without it, it is unclear whether 9–15% is near the achievable floor.
At what steps did the adaptive trigger fire on each pair, and how many post-switch on-policy batches did each adaptive run receive versus fixed_switch_1500?
Can you provide the per-pair val_invalid_rate table for all six arms so readers can compute their own paired intervals?
Why was seed confounded with fold rather than crossing them, given that variance attribution is central to the discussion?

Does the pure_on_policy outlier pair (23.2) correspond to collapse onto a single mode, a mode-mixing failure, or something else? Even one decoded-mode histogram would address the stated competing explanation.
Given that two controls failed and the hard-label baseline was not re-run, what is the intended takeaway for someone designing a distillation schedule?
What numeric seed SD was used for the falsification threshold: the adaptive arm's (2.23), the better pure arm's (8.48), or a pooled value?
Do saved checkpoints exist for a post-hoc mode-share analysis of greedy decodes per arm? This would test the mode-commitment hypothesis without retraining.
At what steps did the adaptive trigger fire on each pair? How do those steps relate to the pure_on_policy outcomes on the same folds?
Why was the yoked arm assigned seed+1000 rather than the same seed? Was the intention to break the dependence on initialisation?
Is the 8.8 hard-label baseline from the same student, folds and step budget? If so, every distillation arm underperforms plain hard-label training, which is itself a notable finding worth discussing.

feedback.text: Keep the plan from the last round. Setup cites limit_15 and limit_16 for what was not recorded; do not ask for those details. Apply the panel's suggestions: let the limitations stand as written without added examples, put the six-arm means first in Results, account for every registered prediction in Results, and explain withdrawn claims once.
